details:
**Xi Jinping**
The leader of the People's Republic of China, who succeeded Hu Jintao as Communist Party General Secretary in 2012 and as President in 2013. He is a "princeling" (the son of revolutionary leader Xi Zhongxun), and as a young official he visited Muscatine, Iowa, in 1985 with an agricultural delegation; nearly every question ends with "led by Xi Jinping."

**Zero-COVID policy**
China's strict pandemic strategy, officially called "dynamic clearing," relied on mass lockdowns, quarantine camps, and frequent PCR testing (often every 72 hours) to stamp out every outbreak. China abruptly relaxed it in December 2022, and as cases surged while official counts denied a rise, the U.S. and EU countries began requiring negative COVID tests from travelers arriving from China.

**A4 Revolution (white paper protests)**
Nationwide protests in November 2022 against zero-COVID, set off by a deadly apartment fire in Urumqi, Xinjiang, that killed at least ten people and was blamed on lockdown measures. Protesters held up blank sheets of A4 paper to symbolize censorship. A month earlier, a lone protester hung banners on Beijing's Sitong Bridge denouncing Xi as a dictator and traitor and broadcast "we want to eat, we want freedom, we want to vote."

**Uyghurs and Xinjiang**
China has detained an estimated one million or more Uyghur Muslims and other minorities in "re-education camps" in the northwestern Xinjiang region, drawing accusations of crimes against humanity and genocide. In December 2020 the U.S. banned cotton imports from the XPCC (Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps), a paramilitary conglomerate linked to forced labor.

**Belt and Road Initiative**
Xi's global infrastructure program, under which China has spent hundreds of billions of dollars on ports, railways, and roads abroad. China has also been accused of secretly building a naval base for its own use at Cambodia's Ream Naval Base.

**Alibaba, Singles' Day, and Ant Group**
Alibaba is the Chinese e-commerce giant founded by Jack Ma, whose 2014 New York listing was the largest IPO in U.S. stock market history. It turned "Singles' Day" (November 11) into the world's biggest online shopping event, and its financial affiliate Ant Group had its record IPO suspended at the last minute in November 2020 as regulators cracked down on Ma's businesses.

**Tencent and WeChat**
Tencent is the Chinese tech giant that developed WeChat, the dominant messaging and payment app in China, and owns the web portal QQ. WeChat Pay and Alibaba's Alipay let users send each other digital "red envelopes" of money, a modern version of a Lunar New Year tradition.

**Huawei and Meng Wanzhou**
Huawei is China's largest telecom equipment maker, and its subsidiary HiSilicon designs its chips. Its CFO Meng Wanzhou, daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei, was arrested in Canada in 2018 at the request of the U.S. over charges related to violating sanctions on Iran, and she spent nearly three years under house arrest in Vancouver.

**ByteDance and TikTok**
ByteDance is the Beijing-based developer of TikTok. In 2020 the Trump administration tried to force the sale of TikTok's U.S. operations, with Oracle and Walmart nearly acquiring them, and India banned TikTok and over 200 other Chinese apps after a deadly border clash with China.

**Evergrande and the property crisis**
Evergrande was once China's largest real estate developer, but it collapsed under more than $300 billion in debt beginning in 2021, symbolizing a wider property crisis. In 2021, the city of Kunming demolished fifteen unfinished apartment towers of the stalled Sunshine City II project.

**Disputes with Japan**
China and Japan dispute the Senkaku Islands (called the Diaoyu Islands in China), with frequent incursions by Chinese coast guard ships. Other flashpoints include Japanese officials' visits to the Yasukuni Shrine, which honors war criminals, the portrayal of the Rape of Nanking in Japanese textbooks, and China's 2023 ban on Japanese seafood after Japan began releasing treated water from the Fukushima nuclear plant.

**Bo Xilai and Neil Heywood**
Bo Xilai was the powerful Communist Party chief of Chongqing and a rising princeling. His downfall began in 2012 when his wife, Gu Kailai, was convicted of murdering the British businessman Neil Heywood, and in 2013 Bo was sentenced to life in prison for bribery, embezzlement, and abuse of power.

**Chen Guangcheng**
A blind, self-taught legal activist who exposed forced abortions under China's one-child policy. In April 2012 he escaped house arrest and took refuge in the U.S. embassy in Beijing, causing a diplomatic crisis before he was allowed to leave for the United States.

**Princelings and the "Fifth Generation"**
"Princelings" are the children of senior Communist Party revolutionaries, and Xi's Fifth Generation of leadership (following Mao's First Generation, then Deng, Jiang Zemin, and Hu Jintao) was dominated by them. In 2013 the U.S. SEC began investigating J.P. Morgan's "Sons and Daughters" program for hiring princelings to win business in China.

**Deng Xiaoping's "cat theory" and Special Economic Zones**
Deng Xiaoping, China's leader after Mao, justified market reforms with the saying "it doesn't matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice." His reforms created Special Economic Zones and other development zones such as Hainan and Shanghai's Pudong, leading to the rapid growth that made China the world's second-largest economy after it passed Japan in 2010.
